https://www.politico.eu/article/palantir.text: Palantir is shifting profits from its European operations to the United States, allowing the Florida-based data analytics giant to pay minimal taxes in Europe, a new report finds. The report by the U.K.-based Centre for International Corporate Tax Accountability and Research, a group partly funded by labor unions that researches corporate tax avoidance in an effort to win reform of global tax rules, found that Palantir’s European subsidiaries, which took in €440.5 million in annual revenue in 2024, report far smaller profit margins in Europe than in the U.S. “Although a substantial part of Palantir’s revenue is realized in Europe, almost all of the pre-tax profits are funneled to the United States,” the report said. Advertisement Advertisement Palantir pays no U.S. federal income tax because previous losses, tax credits, and R&D deductions offset its taxable income; and virtually no state income tax, with the exception of Maryland, which levies a digital services tax. The profit gap between the U.S. and Europe is stark. In 2025, Palantir’s American business pocketed 47.7 cents in profit from every dollar of revenue — more than double the previous year’s 22.5 cents. Outside the U.S., the profit margin was just 6.3 percent. In some European subsidiaries, it fell to around 3 percent, according to the new report. CICTAR argues that Palantir "intentionally and artificially" shrinks European profits — and therefore its European tax bills — to concentrate profits in the U.S. There is no claim in the report that such arrangements, often referred to as "profit shifting," are illegal. Multinational companies often reduce reported profits by paying subsidiaries or other related entities for intellectual property, loans or expertise. In Sweden, for example, Palantir reported €13.7 million in revenue in 2024, but only €1.1 million in profit. At Sweden’s 20 percent corporate tax rate, that left the company with a tax bill of just €424,000. In its Q2 earnings report on Monday, Palantir made no explicit reference to earnings from its European subsidiaries. Instead, it highlighted its U.S. business, where revenue rose 115 percent year-on-year to $1.57 billion (€1.36 billion), and boasted of its 62 percent profit margin. A U.K.-based Palantir spokesperson said that the majority of the company's 2025 revenue and profitability was driven by its U.S. business. "Our tax position in each jurisdiction reflects the level of economic activity there, and we meet our tax obligations in every market in which we operate," the spokesperson said. Advertisement Advertisement Not alone Palantir is not the first U.S. tech company to draw scrutiny over how it books profits in Europe. In 2024, the European Court of Justice ordered Apple to pay Ireland €13 bn in back taxes, ending an 8-year-long fight over what Brussels said amounted to illegal state aid. Amazon also fought the European Commission over claims it had received an unlawful tax advantage worth around €250 million in Luxembourg — a case the company ultimately won . Microsoft, meanwhile, has faced scrutiny over its Irish subsidiary, Microsoft Round Island One, which avoided paying millions to the state after claiming tax residency in Bermuda. The U.S. software giant has denied that it is circumventing Ireland's tax laws. Jan Willem Goudriaan, General Secretary of the European Federation of Public Service Unions — a supporter of CICTAR— said that companies such as Palantir, Amazon and Microsoft focus on minimizing the taxes they pay, "thus robbing funding for public services." "Companies bidding for public contracts should have to demonstrate responsible tax conduct by disclosing where their revenues, workforce, profits and taxes are located," he said. Another reason for the low profits of Palantir’s European subsidiaries is their high personnel costs. In the U.K., where most of the company’s non-U.S. workforce is based, Palantir reported £173 million (€204.3 million) in employee costs for 749 staff in 2024 — an average of £230,974 (€272,803) per employee. The report also points to Palantir’s use of stock-based compensation across its European subsidiaries, especially in the U.K., Spain and Norway. This means employees are paid partly in company shares or awards. Those awards are recorded as staff expenses, which can lower a subsidiary’s corporate tax bill. Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: Sánchez addresses parliament on the government's handling of a massive border breach in the Spanish territory of Ceuta. Photograph: Olmo Blanco/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Sánchez addresses parliament on the government's handling of a massive border breach in the Spanish territory of Ceuta. Photograph: Olmo Blanco/Getty Images Spain Spain’s PM says no evidence ‘whatsoever’ Morocco behind Ceuta border breach Pedro Sánchez continues to defend Rabat after police report claiming border forces helped 70,000 cross border Europe live – latest updates Stephen Burgen in Barcelona Thu 3 Sep 2026 08.52 EDT Last modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 08.58 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Spain has seen no evidence “whatsoever” that Morocco planned or facilitated a mass border breach into its north African territory of Ceuta, the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez , has told parliament. The address on Thursday followed the emergence of a police report, commissioned by a judge and widely quoted in the media, claiming Moroccan border forces had actively aided about 70,000 people to cross the border in late July. “I ‌can assure you ‌that no institution – not the diplomatic service, nor the European Commission , ‌nor any international body – has provided the Spanish government with any solid evidence that Morocco planned or carried out the incident. None whatsoever,” Sánchez told parliament. Speaking the morning after about 50,000 people marched in Madrid to protest his handling of the Ceuta crisis, the socialist prime minister also denied the government had received any warning of the mass breach, saying no reports to authorities had anticipated “the scale or probability of what eventually happened”. View image in fullscreen A protest against the Spanish government’s handling of the recent border breach at Ceuta. Photograph: Francesco Militello Mirto/NurPhoto/Shutterstock Sánchez has repeatedly defended Morocco during the crisis, highlighting Rabat’s cooperation in returning most of the migrants in the days after the surge. But he said on Thursday that Spain had summoned Morocco’s ambassador on 21 August because of “unacceptable statements” made by two ministers over Ceuta and Melilla, another Spanish north African territory. Last month, Morocco’s justice minister, Abdellatif Ouahbi, publicly reiterated Rabat’s sovereignty claims over the cities. Sánchez said he had “for now” ruled out Moroccan government involvement but conceded that Moroccan forces had allowed crossings to occur during a key 10-hour period on 30 July. Many of those who crossed said in interviews they had been actively encouraged to do so. Moroccan officials have denied enabling the crossing. Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party, called on Sánchez to resign for his “incompetence and complicity”. In response to Sánchez summoning the Moroccan ambassador to discuss the crisis, Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, said: “Morocco doesn’t need an ambassador in Spain – you are its ambassador.” View image in fullscreen People who entered Ceuta from Morocco in late July on hunger strike last month to demand asylum. Photograph: Laura Rincon/EPA As many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to enter Ceuta at the end of July. The influx unleashed a political crisis, a humanitarian emergency and reignited tensions within the EU over immigration . On Thursday, Sánchez appealed for European solidarity over the crisis. He did not single out any countries by name but, in a pointed passage apparently aimed at Italy and Denmark, the two countries that had led public criticism of Spain, said the principle of solidarity should apply to Ceuta as much as it applies to Greenland and Lampedusa. Ceuta showed just how easily Europe can be divided Read more Although 90% of the people had returned to Morocco within 24 hours, several thousand, including at least 500 minors, are thought to remain, either living on the street or in makeshift shelters. Amid calls from Vox to return them to Morocco, Sánchez reminded parliament that under Spanish, European and international law, migrants had a right to be treated as individuals. “You can’t just grab someone by the arm and drag them across the frontier as though they were a sack of dirt,” he told MPs. In reference to the hundreds of destitute minors, Aina Vidal of the leftwing group Sumar, said: “They’re children, not invaders, not soldiers. They didn’t come carrying bombs, they arrived wearing water wings, in tears.” ‘We want to find a better future’: teenage girls on why they risked their lives to reach Spain Read more It seems likely the government will invest in facilities in Ceuta to accommodate the remaining migrants rather than risk the political backlash both in Spain and across Europe were they to bring them to the mainland. There is also evidence that, faced with hunger as well as hostility from many local people, some migrants have already begun going back to Morocco. However, as Sánchez told parliament, the per capita income of Ceuta is eight times that of Morocco and “even if we build a wall 100 metres high there will still be people prepared to throw themselves into the sea to get across”. “We will not stop working until Ceuta emerges from this difficult situation: stronger, more prosperous, and more integrated with the rest of Spain and the EU,” he added. Beállítom Seven out of ten Hungarian voters believe that corruption was organized centrally and systematically, from the top down during the NER era, and a majority view certain highly successful entrepreneurs as Viktor Orbán’s front men, according to a Medián survey published on Hvg.hu . NER is short for Nemzeti Együttműködés Rendszere, meaning ’System of National Cooperation.’ The term was coined by the Orbán government after their election victory in 2010 to refer to the changes in government that they were about to introduce. The term later became a word in its own right, and has been used in colloquial Hungarian to refer to Fidesz' governing elite, complete with the politicians and the oligarchs profiting from the system. Three-quarters of the country’s voting-age population believe that financial misuse was widespread in the Orbán government: 60 percent say it was very widespread, and another 15 percent say it was widespread. Opinions mainly vary according to age, educational attainment, and party preference: 82 percent of those under 30 consider the abuse to have been very extensive, while among those over 65, this proportion is 46 percent. Those with higher levels of education are significantly more critical than those with only a primary school education. Fifty-six percent of the Hungarian population considers it very likely, and another 29 percent considers it conceivable that certain exceptionally successful entrepreneurs were Viktor Orbán’s front men. Overall, 85 percent of respondents do not rule out this possibility, and even 5 percent of Fidesz supporters find it very likely. Those who participated in the survey conducted in late July were asked, “Which term best describes the system of government under Viktor Orbán?” and could choose from seven options. The majority—37 percent of respondents—chose the term “mafia state,” while “civic democracy” received 15 percent and “autocracy” 14 percent. As a second choice, “autocracy” ranked first (19 percent), followed by “dictatorship” (17 percent) and “mafia state” (16 percent). Put together, the first and second mentions show that the interpretation of the system as a “mafia state” has increased significantly since 2023, rising from 34 to 53 percent.
